newsitem.title: India: India Reliance posts 1:1 bonus share issue.
newsitem.headline: India Reliance posts 1:1 bonus share issue.

text.p: Reliance Industries, India's leading private firm, on Thursday announced a one-for-one bonus share issue, and said it did not foresee any further equity dilution during the next two to three years.

The announcement, given by Dhirubhal Ambani, chairman of the petrochemical and textile giant, to a packed annual general meeting of shareholders surpassed earlier expectations, although some analysts had expected the generous 1:1 bonus.
Earlier traders had expected the company to announce a bonus ratio of three shares for every five shares held -- the same ratio as the firm's last two bonus issues in the 1980s.
Ambani had earlier told the AGM not to expect further dilution of the company's equity over the next few years.
"We do not foresee any further equity dilution over the next two to three years, excluding outstanding conversions (of debentures)," he said.
At 0830 GMT, the Reliance share was up 12 rupees at 378.50 rupees on the Bombay stock exchange, up 3.3 percent.
Reliance began as a commodities trading firm in 1958 and built itself into India's largest private company.
Ambani said the company's sales were expected to touch 200 billion rupees ($5.5 billion) by 2000.
"Based on firm plans, our sales are expected to approach the 200 billion rupees milestone by the year 2000," he said.
"We have set ourselves targets of achieving 20 percent compound growth in earnings per share and a return of 20 percent on shareholders funds over the next five years," Ambani said.
Beginning this year Reliance plans to follow international accounting practices.
"We will also be reconciling our accounts in line with U.S. GAAP (general accepted accounting principles) standards from the current year," Ambani said.
This will be in addition to Indian accounting standards, he said, adding the firm had a global investor base.
Since 1992, Reliance has raised $1.5 billion from international markets that included global depositary receipts (GDRs), Euro bonds, and a 100-year maturity bond in the U.S. ($1.00=35.82 rupees)
